## Methods: How do we answer questions?

The research method:

Start with a question

State a hypothesis

Collect data

Use your data to test your hypothesis

## State a Hypothesis

Define and operationalize your variables:

Make a hypothesis about the relationship between the variables:

_“If a speaker is from a state in the Midwest, then they’ll be more likely to use the word “pop” to describe carbonated drinks.” _

Region:

State of origin

Variant:

Soda, pop, coke, fizzy drink, soft drink, etc.

Dependent variable

Independent variable

::: {.notes}

Operationalizing a variable makes it measurable - you’re defining the potential values it can have
You have to be strategic. 
Region: 
How specific? Country / state / county / city / home address. Based on our question, what makes the most sense? 
When? Where someone was born? Where they live now? Where they spent the most time? 


In this example, region is the independent variable (the variable we think is affecting the linguistic behavior) and variant is the dependent variable (the variable we think is affected by changes in region). 
You might have multiple hypotheses
Note: this hypothesis is still pretty unspecific. What’s the “Midwest”?




:::

## Methods of collecting data:

Experiments

Participants are divided into a control group and experimental group(s)

Researchers manipulate the independent variable(s) and then measure the dependent variable(s)

Surveys

Participants respond to a prepared set of questions

Participants are sampled from a population of interest

Participant observation

Researchers observe people in their daily routines

Often, this method is exploratory and descriptive

Existing resources

Researchers use existing data collected by others (e.g. government agencies or other researchers)

::: {.notes}

For the carbonated drinks question: 
Population: Americans English speakers
Sample: 
Survey with questions targeting: 
The speaker’s word for a carbonated/fizzy drink ?
Some variant of “where are you from?”  depending on how you define the region variable



:::

## surveys



* The phrasing and order of questions can be important!
  * Yes/No vs. Multiple choice vs. Open-ended
  * Order of questions
  * Phrasing of questions
* What’s your word for “pop”?
* Which word do you use:  “soda” or “pop”?
* What’s your generic term for a sweetened carbonated beverage?

## Blorp

https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2021/04/19/how-did-a-self-taught-linguist-come-to-own-an-indigenous-language

::: {.notes}

There’s a lot to unpack from this article, but key points: 
Who was this research for? 

This research has had benefits for the Penobscot community
Language revitalization efforts make use of Siebert’s wordlists and dictionary.
Carol Dana leads lessons and activities with students, trains instructors, helped the Penobscot Theatre Company stage a production of Gluskabe stories starring local children
Conor Quinn, Siebert’s former assistant, leads summer language intensives for local teenagers and has been working to revise the Penobscot dictionary

But Frank Siebert didn’t necessarily have the community in mind
The data he collected didn’t belong to the community (it was legally his under copyright law, and then the American Philosophical Society’s)



“ Anderson sees Siebert’s approach as archetypal of nineteenth- and early-twentieth-century anthropological research, which tended to cast indigenous people not as participants but as objects of study, and rarely aspired to benefit them.” 
Siebert’s research, including the language data he collected, does not belong to the community that made it possible (and that could benefit most from it)
“ In copying down the grammar, the stories, and the vocabulary of the Penobscot, Siebert made them his. In dying, he made them the American Philosophical Society’s.” 

One part of the article describes Siebert interviewing a group of elders and correcting one of them, claiming more knowledge of the Penobscot language than the people he’s interviewing (prescriptivism vs. descriptivism)


:::

## What do you need for ethical research?

Informed consent or permission to use existing data

A plan for storing and future use of data

Minimal risk of harm to participants  _or_  mitigation strategies if unavoidable

Only collect the information you need to answer your question(s)

Accountability and oversight

::: {.notes}

We’ve seen lots of unethical ways to do research. So 


- There are relationships between these five things, which we’ll see


:::

## Informed Consent

“I have a few questions to ask you about how you feel about Southern accents. The interview will be audio recorded and should take no more than 20 minutes. Your data will be confidential, and the data will be anonymized prior to storage. The data may be used in future experiments. You may withdraw your consent at any time. Do you agree to participate in the research?”

::: {.notes}

Informed consent  
includes: as much transparency as possible
Mentions any risk of harm to the participant



Contrast with: Milgram experiment (“you may withdraw your consent at any time”)


Confidentiality / Anonymity: also a way of minimizing risk of harm to participants





:::

## Permission to use Existing Data

Anything that has been published is generally acceptable for academic use,  _unless it contains other restrictions or could cause harm to private individuals_ .

## ACCOUNTABILITY AND oversight

![](images/13-SPOTLIGHT%202%20-%20Methods%20and%20Ethics_22.png)

![](images/13-SPOTLIGHT%202%20-%20Methods%20and%20Ethics_23.jpg)

![](images/13-SPOTLIGHT%202%20-%20Methods%20and%20Ethics_24.png)

![](images/13-SPOTLIGHT%202%20-%20Methods%20and%20Ethics_25.png)

::: {.notes}

Many universities require training before allowing scholars to conduct research
The IRB exists to ensure the research being conducted at an institutional is being done ethically
Before conducting research, researchers submit a proposal to the IRB
The IRB assesses the level of risk to the subjects, and the researcher’s plan at all stages (recruitment, data collection, data storage / destruction, etc)

:::
